narrativeImpact.story: Two months later... you stabilize IMC by pairing Tasha’s early-career leadership with Thomas’s operational backbone, while setting clear expectations for the remaining team. Three external hires bring analytics and AI-enabled workflow discipline, reducing rework loops and shortening toolkit cycle time. Denise’s transition is handled with time-bound knowledge capture to protect partner trust. With a clearer intake path and modern capabilities, cross-functional teams stop bypassing process, and your influence grows as execution tightens.
narrativeImpact.title: Alignment in Motion
narrativeImpact.description: The team is starting to gel. Communication is thoughtful, and team members are starting to operate with greater confidence and cohesion. There’s still work ahead, but momentum is building.

narrativeImpact.story: Two months later... you completed the transition checklist, but the team’s pace stayed flat. With Ron, you logged priorities without converting them into ownership or deadlines; follow-ups were sporadic. With Susan, you gathered input but didn’t translate it into clear decisions or visible wins. Work kept moving, yet no one rallied around a shared cadence. In the reorg’s wake, execution remained steady—while your influence plateaued amid competing agendas.
narrativeImpact.title: Stable, but Stalled
narrativeImpact.description: Team lacks energy, purpose, and follow-through.  The transition is technically complete — but momentum is missing.

narrativeImpact.story: Two months later... you stabilized IMC by retaining a core team to keep intake, timelines, and approvals moving while stripping out redundant “double-check” work. Malek was tasked to publish a weekly campaign scorecard pulling media, ecommerce, and Insights data, accelerating test-and-learn. A new player-coach leader embedded AI-enabled reporting and cross-training, reducing reliance on hand-carried decks. Launches stayed steady, and your influence grew as decisions became faster and measurable.

narrativeImpact.story: Two months later, you’ve reshaped IMC into a faster, measurable launch engine. Thomas sets an execution cadence that reinforces AI adoption, while Denise stabilizes intake and keeps brand partners aligned. Malek and Tasha accelerate tool usage and iteration, and Jules raises the creative bar without derailing delivery. narrativeImpact.title: Built to Thryve
narrativeImpact.description: Your actions spark clarity, conviction, and alignment. The team understands not just what’s changing — but why. People feel seen, empowered, and focused. New capabilities are beginning to take hold, and Thryve’s marketing function is positioned to compete, evolve, and lead. The way forward is not just clear — it's energized.

Cross-training became two-way, pairing institutional trust with AI-enabled workflows and tighter measurement. Small, visible milestones proved the “bus is moving” message, shortening cycle times and improving stakeholder confidence. With a repeatable content engine in-market, you became a reliable force shaping Thryve’s modern marketing cadence.

events.content: Chapter 1: Chapter 1: Survive... or Thryve? has started.

What is this chapter about?
Teams play the role of a new leader of the Brand Marketing team at Thryve, a global consumer packaged goods company. Just before their start date, the leader of the Integrated Marketing Communications (IMC) team was promoted, and a decision was made to roll up the IMC team's functionality under Brand Marketing. The IMC team has 8 members, but teams only have headcount for 6. They must ultimately decide whether to eliminate the IMC team entirely, to keep some members and to use the remaining available headcount for new hires, or to keep 6 members of the IMC team and delay additional hiring. In this first chapter, teams interview Ron, the former leader of the IMC team, to get his perspective.

What to look for:
  • Do teams explore how the IMC team's structure and responsibilities align with the organization's overall goals?
  • Do they explore the structural implications of their decision?
  • Do they surface any potential skill and capability gaps?

Chapter 2: Chapter 2: Built to Thryve. has started.

What is this chapter about?
Teams now use a tool to build the new organizational structure of their department. They must decide which team members from IMC to bring over to Brand Marketing, and which to send to HR for reassignment elsewhere in the company. Teams have access to Ron still if they have any followup questions.

What to look for:
  • Do teams make their decision on time within the tool?
  • Do teams have a clear rationale for their decision? (You might need to listen in on conversations to discover this.)

Chapter 3: Chapter 3: Time to Thryve! has started.

What is this chapter about?
Teams meet with their boss, Susan, to explain their recommendation. Susan will push teams to articulate how their approach connects to Thryve's strategy, structure, and skill needs.

What to look for:
  • Do they discuss how to implement their plan (communication, clarifying roles, supporting affected team members)?
  • Do they discuss what their decision will mean for people or work that is impacted (emotions, performance, team culture)?
  • Do teams explore what their recommendation says about their priorities, values, or leadership style?
Remember to move around to listen to teams' discussions. Sometimes the most insightful comments are said from one participant to another, rather than to an AI character.
